evidence.content: As inflation moved closer to the Bank’s target range by 2024, policymakers initiated a cautious easing phase. Rate cuts were small and widely spaced, reflecting the Bank's concern that inflation pressures—although declining—were not yet fully extinguished. At the same time, keeping the policy rate unchanged for too long risked tightening financial conditions further in real terms, given falling inflation. [...] Through its policy tools, the Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation, measured by changes in the CPI, within an optimal range. Established in 1991, the inflation-control target is set at 1% to 3%, with a midpoint target of 2% as the preferred rate for annual inflation. This target range is reviewed periodically (typically every 5 years), with the latest review conducted in 2021 and the next review coming up in 2026. [...] After reaching its peak, the Bank kept the policy rate unchanged for an extended period. Maintaining the rate at this restrictive level allowed the full impact of earlier tightening to work through the economy. Inflation decelerated steadily as supply chains normalized, energy prices cooled, and domestic demand softened.

🎥 🍿 📺   
Just a heads up in case you didn’t know about Netflix’s price changes…  
  
For a while, their Standard plan sat at $15.49 and it stayed at that price for about 2 years before any increase.  
  
Then in 2025, it jumped to $17.99.  
  
Now in 2026, it’s being raised again to $19.99.  
  
That’s a $4.50 increase in just a couple years, after being steady for quite a while. [...] It also includes FilmBox, which is nice because I can watch shows like Outlander that are normally only on platforms like Starz, plus other shows that are usually locked behind different subscriptions.  
  
Streaming used to feel like the cheaper alternative… but with prices continuing to climb like this, it can definitely start to add up. Anyone rethinking their subscriptions lately? 👀  
  
P.s We only pay for Netflix
